source.title: An Investigation Into the Relationship Between Maximum Isometric Strength and Vertical Jump Performance

paper.citation: Thomas C., Jones P.A., Rothwell J., Chiang C.Y., Comfort P. An Investigation Into the Relationship Between Maximum Isometric Strength and Vertical Jump Performance. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2015;29(8):2176-2185. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000000866.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: How are maximal isometric strength variables associated with squat-jump and countermovement-jump force, power, velocity, and height, and do relatively stronger collegiate athletes outperform weaker peers? Participants: 22 male collegiate athletes, age 21.3±2.9 years, height 175.63±8.23 cm, mass 78.06±10.77 kg. Sport and level: Collegiate cricket, judo, rugby, and soccer. Design: Cross-sectional correlational study with a secondary median-split comparison. Exposure or intervention: IMTP peak force, maximum rate of force development, impulses at 100/200/300 ms, and total impulse.
paper.tldr: Absolute IMTP impulses at 100–300 ms correlated with CMJ peak force (r=.63–.64, p≤.01), SJ peak force (r=.56–.58, p≤.01), CMJ peak power (r=.49–.51, p≤.05), and SJ peak power (r=.59–.60, p≤.01); correlations with jump height were near zero and nonsignificant. Stronger and weaker groups differed in relative IMTP peak force (38.72±2.08 vs 30.40±4.01 N/kg, p=.01, d=2.60) and relative maximum RFD (172.59±37.64 vs 103.12±35.95 N/kg/s, p=.01, d=1.89). IMTP impulse and absolute force can complement jump peak-force and peak-power profiling, but they should not be treated as substitutes for jump height or dynamic performance.
paper.methods: Design: Cross-sectional correlational study with a secondary median-split comparison. Exposure or intervention: IMTP peak force, maximum rate of force development, impulses at 100/200/300 ms, and total impulse. Comparator: IMTP variables versus squat-jump and countermovement-jump variables; strongest n=11 versus weakest n=11 by relative peak force. Measurements and outcomes: Force-platform peak velocity, peak force, peak power, and flight-time jump height. Analysis: Pearson correlations; independent t tests and Cohen's d for group comparisons; significance p≤.05.
paper.findings: Absolute IMTP impulses at 100–300 ms correlated with CMJ peak force (r=.63–.64, p≤.01), SJ peak force (r=.56–.58, p≤.01), CMJ peak power (r=.49–.51, p≤.05), and SJ peak power (r=.59–.60, p≤.01); correlations with jump height were near zero and nonsignificant. Stronger and weaker groups differed in relative IMTP peak force (38.72±2.08 vs 30.40±4.01 N/kg, p=.01, d=2.60) and relative maximum RFD (172.59±37.64 vs 103.12±35.95 N/kg/s, p=.01, d=1.89). They did not differ significantly in CMJ height (0.33±0.05 vs 0.36±0.05 m, p=.19) or SJ height (0.29±0.06 vs 0.33±0.05 m, p=.14). Relative IMTP impulse measures were not significantly associated with vertical-jump performance measures in this sample.
paper.limitations: The small, homogeneous, mixed-sport male sample limits precision and sport-specific transfer. Jump height derived from flight time can be influenced by takeoff and landing body configuration. Maximum RFD showed high variability (%CV=15.1), and findings depended on the sampling/scaling method. Additional causal limitation — interpretation: Correlations do not show that increasing IMTP impulse will cause improved jump performance.
paper.practicalImplications: IMTP impulse and absolute force can complement jump peak-force and peak-power profiling, but they should not be treated as substitutes for jump height or dynamic performance. In collegiate American football, the study is best used to reinforce construct specificity and the need for stable within-athlete methods, not as a source of sport-specific cut points.

paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, iMTP impulse and absolute force can complement jump peak-force and peak-power profiling, but they should not be treated as substitutes for jump height or dynamic performance. In collegiate American football, the study is best used to reinforce construct specificity and the need for stable within-athlete methods, not as a source of sport-specific cut points. Use the paper as one input to interdisciplinary judgment, not as a standalone clearance criterion or reinjury prediction rule.
